extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates, graduate students, and mathematically literate readers interested in history and foundations of analysis
extracted.subtask_description: An expository textbook chapter tracing the historical and conceptual development of nonstandard (infinitesimal) analysis and Fourier analysis, emphasizing issues of rigor, formal language, and what counts as a valid mathematical argument. The material targets readers learning about foundations and methods in analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weierstrass (epsilon-delta) definition of limit/velocity
rubrics_metrics.description: Define instantaneous velocity as a limit approximated by ratios of finite increments: given variable finite increments Δt and Δs, Δs/Δt can be made arbitrarily close to the speed v; formalized by the epsilon-delta condition (“The velocity is v if, for any positive number ε, Δs/Δt − v is less than ε in absolute value for all values of Δt less in absolute value than some other positive number δ (which depends on ε and t)).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This removes reference to nonfinite numbers and the direct setting of Δt = 0. It requires the reader/writer to state quantifiers (for every ε there exists δ) explicitly. Note: unintuitive at first but accepted as rigorous; relies on training to use naturally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid informal infinitesimal manipulations unless formalized (Berkeley critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Berkeley criticised reasoning that treats increments as 'evanescent' and then drops 'negligible' terms (e.g., setting dt to zero after differentiating), calling them 'ghosts of departed quantities.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: treating Δt as simultaneously nonzero (to compute ratios) and zero (to drop terms). Acceptable practice is either (a) use rigorous epsilon-delta limits or (b) adopt a formal nonstandard framework that distinguishes nonstandard quantities from their standard parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalizability as a test of understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: "The possibility of putting a mathematical discovery into a formal language is the test of whether it is fully understood."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for evaluating mathematical clarity: if a concept or proof can be translated into an explicit formal language (with precise semantics), it is taken as fully understood. Use this as a desideratum when proposing definitions or proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of formal language and model theory (truth and models)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat mathematics via a formal language L whose sentences about a standard universe M are either true or false. The set K of all true sentences has M as a model; other structures M* can also be models for K (nonstandard models).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing foundationally, make explicit what formal language and interpretation you are using, and clarify whether statements are intended as sentences of L and which model (standard or nonstandard) is meant. This controls which properties are preserved under interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of nonstandard models via compactness theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Compactness theorem: if every finite subset of a collection of sentences of L is true in the standard universe, then there exists a (possibly nonstandard) universe in which the entire collection is true; this can be used to produce infinitesimals (pseudoreals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To justify invoking infinitesimals rigorously, exhibit the logical construction (via compactness/completeness) that yields a nonstandard model in which a new symbol obeys the desired infinite-family constraints. This is the accepted method to show 'existence' of infinitesimals in the model-theoretic sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressibility constraint: only L-expressible properties transfer to nonstandard models
rubrics_metrics.description: Properties expressible in the formal language L hold both in the standard universe and in nonstandard models for the same sentences; properties requiring infinitely many sentences (e.g., the Archimedean property) may fail in a nonstandard model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming that a nonstandard model preserves some feature of the standard model, check that the feature is expressible as a single sentence of L. If it requires an infinite schema, it may not transfer, and that difference is exactly what permits infinitesimals to exist in the nonstandard model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence requirement for nonstandard methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonstandard (infinitesimal) methods are acceptable provided they give the same answers as standard methods for statements about standard objects; one must prove that the nonstandard definitions (e.g., instantaneous velocity as the standard part of a ratio) agree with Weierstrass definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using nonstandard techniques to prove theorems about standard objects, include or cite a proof of equivalence to classical definitions/results (so that the nonstandard argument is not only elegant but also mathematically legitimate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish nonstandard quantities from their standard parts
rubrics_metrics.description: In nonstandard analysis, quantities like ds, dt and their ratio ds/dt are nonstandard real numbers; the physically meaningful instantaneous velocity v is the standard part of ds/dt (e.g., ds/dt = 32 + 16 dt, so the standard part v = 32).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state when you are taking the standard part of a pseudonumber. This distinction avoids the Berkeley-type contradiction and must be maintained throughout nonstandard proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt methods that yield insight or simplification
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical justification for nonstandard methods is that embedding standard objects in a nonstandard enlargement can lead to much shorter and more 'insightful' proofs; the method is judged useful if it simplifies arguments or solves previously intractable problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate new methods (nonstandard or otherwise) in part by whether they produce conceptual clarity, shorter proofs, or new results (e.g., applications to dynamics, probability, compact operators). Note that acceptability also depends on the community's willingness to adopt new frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify allowed function class and meaning of infinite sums for Fourier expansions
rubrics_metrics.description: Fourier's theorem requires specifying precisely what functions y are allowed (periodic, piecewise, analytic, etc.) and what is meant by the sum of an infinite series (pointwise, uniform, in mean, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting that a function has a Fourier series or Fourier integral expansion, explicitly state the hypotheses (regularity, periodicity, integrability) and the mode of convergence being claimed; do not assume every graph corresponds to a single-analytic-expression function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify termwise operations on infinite series (integration, summation, rearrangement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier analysts often assumed one could integrate or otherwise manipulate an infinite series term by term; modern standards require justification (e.g., via uniform convergence or Fubini/Tonelli-type theorems) before interchanging summation and integration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns include integrating each term of a nonuniformly-convergent series or rearranging divergent series. When computing coefficients by integrating a supposed expansion, verify conditions that permit termwise integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use orthogonality of sines/cosines to derive Fourier coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: The coefficient formula follows from the orthogonality property: ∫ cos(mx) cos(nx) dx = 0 if m ≠ n (over the appropriate interval).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deriving Fourier coefficients, exploit orthogonality and include the calculation/justification for the orthogonality relations over the chosen interval and inner product; this gives a direct and rigorous route to the coefficient formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unjustified formal manipulations (power series, divergent products)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fourier's original derivation expanded sines in power series, rearranged terms, and divided by a divergent infinite product—formally inconsistent steps that nonetheless led to the correct coefficient formulas by accident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such manipulations as red flags: do not rely on expansions or manipulations that are not justified for the function class at hand. Prefer derivations that use orthogonality, convergence theorems, or other justified analytic tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify what is meant by 'function' (analytic expression vs. piecewise graph)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical dispute: Euler and others thought a 'function' should be a single analytic expression everywhere; Fourier claimed piecewise-defined graphs (temperature distributions given by different formulas on subintervals) should be admitted and have Fourier expansions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State whether you treat functions as single analytic formulas or allow piecewise definitions and discontinuities. Different stances affect which theorems (and which proofs) apply; modern theory provides precise conditions (e.g., piecewise continuity, Dirichlet-like conditions) under which Fourier expansions hold.
